one_line: Callstack engineer Lech Kalinowski builds a handheld text-terminal for OpenClaw and local LLMs on an ESP32, with a thin-client design backed by a 120B model on a DGX Spark. Mostly a hardware showcase with useful field notes.
summary: The speaker, Lech Kalinowski of Callstack, describes a handheld AI terminal built over about three months. It pairs a small OLED screen (live typing) with an e-paper screen (slow, stable display of the final output), driven by an ESP32 dual-core microcontroller. The device is a thin client: a backend on a DGX Spark runs the agent work through OpenClaw and serves an open-source 120B model. Because the MCU has little memory, rendering uses pre-allocated one-bit images with no markdown engine and no malloc. The talk spends a lot of time on hardware problems (I2C pull-ups, a silent GPIO failure, a regulator that damaged the display, and a noisy cheap encoder). The most unusual feature is an RPG mode, where the LLM generates NPCs, worlds and maps that are converted to one-bit assets. The speaker closes with three takeaways and a demo video. Most of the content is a project showcase, with little new detail on LLM serving.

key_ideas.idea: Motivation: a remote controller for an OpenClaw instance on a DGX Spark, with a dual-display design
key_ideas.detail: The speaker wanted a physical device to talk to an LLM. An OLED gives fast typing and an e-paper screen gives a readable, energy-efficient final view. Together they make a low-power terminal.

key_ideas.idea: The device is a thin client; the heavy work runs on a backend
key_ideas.detail: Firmware on the ESP32 handles input and display. A separate backend on the DGX Spark handles the agent work with OpenClaw and the LLM. The MCU does not run models.

key_ideas.idea: On a microcontroller, render from pre-allocated one-bit images
key_ideas.detail: Pages live in fixed buffers in memory. There is no markdown engine and no malloc on the MCU side. The speaker says this is needed because of the memory limits.

key_ideas.idea: Serve an open 120B model behind an OpenAI-style proxy
key_ideas.detail: The speaker ran a 120B open-source model on NVIDIA's serving stack and exposed an OpenAI-style API. Other open models did not match the OpenAI API closely enough, so the proxy was needed to make them work.

key_ideas.idea: Power and hardware issues dominated the build
key_ideas.detail: Silent I2C failure without external pull-ups, a GPIO 13 failure that needed a port move, and a regulator that damaged the display (replacement parts took weeks). Cheap encoders added rotational noise that needed pull-ups and capacitors.

key_ideas.idea: RPG mode uses the LLM for world-building
key_ideas.detail: The LLM generates NPCs, worlds, maps and skills. The images are converted to one-bit matrices so the MCU can display them. The speaker built four worlds and a mood system.

key_ideas.idea: Design for fallbacks so the device stays usable
key_ideas.detail: If the OLED fails, the e-paper still works. If the keyboard fails, the encoder works. If Wi-Fi drops, the local shell still runs.

key_ideas.idea: Takeaways: match displays to the job, LLMs are too heavy for tiny MCUs, and context matters more than numbers
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says no current model runs on very small MCUs, so LLM work must go to a backend. The speaker also says narrative and context matter most for LLM products.

techniques.name: Thin-client MCU with a heavy backend
techniques.how: Keep firmware to input and display only. Put agent orchestration and model calls on a server, and expose it to the device over the network.
techniques.when: When the device has very little RAM or compute and must still feel interactive.

techniques.name: Pre-allocated one-bit page buffers
techniques.how: Store each screen as a fixed one-bit bitmap in memory. Avoid runtime allocation and any markup or layout engine on the MCU.
techniques.when: For text or image output on a small MCU with a monochrome display.

techniques.name: Dual-display split by job
techniques.how: Use a fast OLED for live input and an e-paper panel for a stable, low-power final view that updates only on commit.
techniques.when: When you need fast text entry and a readable, energy-efficient output on the same device.

techniques.name: OpenAI-style proxy in front of open models
techniques.how: Serve an open model with a fast inference engine and wrap it in an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so clients written for the OpenAI API can use it.
techniques.when: When existing agent tooling expects the OpenAI API and the open model's native API does not match it.

techniques.name: Graceful degradation across hardware parts
techniques.how: Give each input and output a fallback path, so the device keeps working if one part fails.
techniques.when: For hardware prototypes where parts are fragile or unreliable.

numbers.claim: About 130 commits over roughly three months of work
Two displays, four modes, four RPG worlds, and 16 character classes
Powered by a single lithium-polymer cell
Backend serves an open-source 120 billion parameter model
MCU is an ESP32 dual-core microcontroller
A GPIO 13 silent failure and an I2C issue without external pull-ups

hot_takes: Match displays to the job. There are plenty on the market.
LLMs are still too heavy for tiny MCUs, so the model has to run on a backend.
Context and narrative matter more than numbers in LLM products.

relevance.why: The speaker found that not all open models match the OpenAI API, so the serving side needed an OpenAI-style proxy. This touches AgentOS's proxy and InferCraft serving, but only lightly.
relevance.action: Check that InferCraft's OpenAI-compatible endpoint works with open models that do not fully match the OpenAI API, and test it with a non-OpenAI-style model.
